chapters.title: Chapter 2: Market Impact and Liquidity: Why Big Money Moves Prices

lessons.title: Case Study: Impact Cost of Buying Rs 5 Crore of a Mid-Cap Nifty Stock

children.text: This chapter has covered order books, the square-root law, and how to measure liquidity properly. This lesson runs all three together on one worked trade, buying Rs 5 crore of a stock from the Nifty Midcap 150 index, and puts an actual rupee number on what impact cost does to a real position.

stats.label: Market cap
stats.context: Free float 40%, so free-float market cap is Rs 4,800 Cr

stats.label: Daily volatility
stats.context: Typical for an actively traded midcap

children.text: The desk wants to buy Rs 5 crore. Using a calibration constant Y of 0.7, consistent with the previous lesson, here is what the square-root model actually predicts.
Rs 5 crore against Rs 25 crore of ADV is a participation ratio of 20 percent if the entire order is executed in a single day, on the higher side of what most desks treat as comfortable.

The square root of 0.20 is about 0.447. Impact cost is 0.7 times 2.2 percent times 0.447, which works out to roughly 0.69 percent of trade value, about Rs 3.44 lakh on a Rs 5 crore order, on the buy side alone.

body.text: A desk that assumes it will transact at the quoted price, zero impact, is off by Rs 3.44 lakh before the position has even had a chance to move in its favor. And this is only one leg. Exiting the position later, assuming similar liquidity conditions, incurs a comparable cost again, so the round-trip impact cost is closer to 1.38 percent of trade value, not 0.69 percent.

children.text: Step 3: Does Spreading the Order Help?

Instead of executing the full Rs 5 crore in one day, split it evenly across 3 trading days. Each day's slice now competes against a fresh day of ADV, so the effective participation ratio for the model becomes Rs 5 crore divided by 3 times Rs 25 crore, which is about 6.67 percent instead of 20 percent.

body.text: Because impact cost follows a square root, spreading an order over N days roughly divides cost by the square root of N, not by N itself. Three days cuts cost by about 42 percent, not 67 percent. This is real money saved, but it is not free: every extra day of execution is an extra day of exposure to the price simply drifting away from you before you finish building the position, a timing risk that Chapter 6's execution algorithms are built to manage.

children.text: What This Means for the Edge

Suppose the strategy behind this trade expects a 4 percent return over the holding period, a perfectly respectable edge on paper. Executed in a single day, the round-trip impact cost of roughly 1.38 percent eats over a third of that edge before brokerage, STT, or any other cost is even considered. Spread over 3 days, round-trip cost falls to roughly 0.80 percent, closer to a fifth of the edge. The strategy did not get better. The execution did.

body.title: Extend the Case Study
body.prompt: Using the same stock (ADV Rs 25 Cr, daily volatility 2.2%, Y = 0.7), if the Rs 5 crore order is spread evenly over 5 trading days instead of 3, what is the estimated impact cost, as a percentage of trade value? Round to two decimals.
body.explanation: Effective participation ratio = 5 / (5 x 25) = 0.04, or 4%. The square root of 0.04 is 0.2. Impact cost = 0.7 x 2.2% x 0.2 = 0.00308, or about 0.31% of trade value, Rs 1.54 lakh on a Rs 5 crore order.

body.text: A single Rs 5 crore trade, in a perfectly ordinary Nifty Midcap 150 stock, can cost over a third of a strategy's expected edge in impact alone if executed carelessly, and roughly halve that cost if spread out sensibly. This is not an edge case. This is the ordinary arithmetic of trading real size.

points: Combining participation ratio with the square-root law converts an abstract liquidity concern into an actual rupee cost estimate for a specific trade.
Round-trip impact cost, buying and later selling, is roughly double the one-leg estimate under similar liquidity conditions, and is easy to underweight if you only think about the entry.
Spreading an order over N days reduces impact cost by roughly the square root of N, a real saving, but one traded off against timing risk over the longer execution window.
Impact cost should always be measured against a strategy's expected edge, not evaluated in isolation, since even a moderate-looking cost can consume a large share of a modest edge.
